blocks.text: Quick verdict

Rayobyte is a solid NetNut replacement for US-focused scraping: it is a US-based vendor, sells ISP and datacenter proxies for former NetNut static users, and its non-expiring residential traffic costs $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB from a terabyte, below NetNut's old rates. The main gap is protocol support: its residential gateway is HTTP(S) only, so tools that used SOCKS5 through NetNut need reconfiguring. Teams needing ASN or carrier targeting should look at a larger network.

Rayobyte vs NetNut used to compare two providers with strong ISP and datacenter roots. Since the FBI seized NetNut's domains in July 2026 after Google linked its network to the Popa botnet, the question is whether Rayobyte can take over NetNut workloads. Rayobyte is a US company with residential, ISP, datacenter and mobile proxies and residential traffic that never expires. This page compares it with NetNut's former offer and explains how to migrate.
What happened to NetNut?

On July 2, 2026, the FBI, working with IRS Criminal Investigation, Google, Lumen and the Shadowserver Foundation, seized hundreds of domains tied to NetNut, the residential proxy service owned by Nasdaq-listed Alarum Technologies. Google's Threat Intelligence Group said NetNut's exit-node pool overlapped with Popa, a botnet it estimated at about two million consumer devices, many of them smart TVs and streaming boxes. Alarum disputes the botnet label and said it would cooperate with law enforcement, but netnut.com and, within days, netnut.io displayed federal seizure notices. As of October 2026 the service is not something you can responsibly buy or rely on.

blocks.text: Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte is a US proxy company that started life as Blazing SEO and built its name on dedicated datacenter proxies. Residential proxies have since become its main product. It sells them pay-as-you-go in four volume bands with traffic that never expires, sources at least part of its residential pool in-house, and offers country, region and city targeting. The notable limit is protocol support: its residential gateway does not support SOCKS5 or UDP.

Rayobyte combines one of the strongest datacenter proxy catalogs with a simple residential offer. Residential traffic is bought in volume bands, from $3.50/GB below 50 GB down to $0.90/GB at a terabyte, and it never expires. Users often praise its human support team. The trade-offs are HTTP-only residential access and limited public data on pool size.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
What NetNut offered, and how Rayobyte compares

Before the seizure, NetNut was best known for ISP-sourced static residential proxies and a fast rotating residential network aimed at scraping, ad verification and brand-protection teams. Its residential rates generally ran from about $1.87 to $3.53 per GB on larger plans, with higher effective prices on entry plans. Rayobyte covers much of the same ground: datacenter (its original strength), isp, mobile, web unblocker, scraping robot sit alongside its residential network, which advertises Not prominently published IPs in Global countries.
What former NetNut customers need, and whether Rayobyte
delivers

Most NetNut accounts were built around three things: static ISP IPs for long-lived sessions, rotating residential traffic with US state and city targeting, and high concurrency for scraping. On static ISP-style IPs, Rayobyte's answer is yes; its other products are datacenter (its original strength), ISP, mobile, Web Unblocker, Scraping Robot. On rotating residential targeting, Rayobyte offers country, region and city in Global countries, with rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available. On billing, Rayobyte uses pay-as-you-go volume bands, and unused traffic is handled as follows: residential traffic does not expire. Map each of your old NetNut zones to one of these before you migrate, so nothing breaks on the day you switch.
Rayobyte pricing
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

Quick cost check for Rayobyte: 10 GB comes to $35 ($3.50/GB), and 100 GB comes to $200 ($2/GB in the 50-249 GB band). NetNut's larger plans used to run about $1.87-$3.53/GB, so compare against what you actually paid rather than NetNut's headline rate.
How to migrate from NetNut to Rayobyte
1. Export your NetNut usage history and list the countries, cities and session types you actually used, so you can map them to Rayobyte's targeting (country, region and city).
2. Test before you commit. Rayobyte's testing option: check current offer. Run your real targets for a day on the smallest purchase before moving production traffic.
3. Swap the gateway host and credentials in your scraper or browser profiles. Rayobyte supports HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential), so tools that relied on SOCKS5 need an HTTP(S) configuration.
4. Compare success rate, response time and cost per successful request against your old NetNut baseline, then move traffic over in stages.
5. Remove any NetNut SDKs, browser extensions or endpoints from your systems, and rotate any credentials that were stored alongside them.
Where Rayobyte fits best
General web scraping: strong fit. Why: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires.
SERP and rank tracking: workable. Why: usable, with no dedicated SERP product.
Social media and multi-account management: workable. Why: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: strong fit. Why: city targeting and low prices at volume.
Ad verification and geo-testing: workable. Why: fewer carrier or ASN controls.
Tight budgets: strong fit. Why: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte.
Protocols and sessions

Rayobyte supports HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential) and offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available. Targeting covers country, region and city across Global countries. Like NetNut's residential gateway, it works through a single backconnect endpoint with location and session options passed in the username, plus IP whitelisting.
How to vet a residential proxy provider after NetNut

NetNut's customers did not choose to route traffic through a botnet; they bought what looked like a standard enterprise service. The lesson is to check sourcing before you buy, not after. Whichever provider replaces NetNut for you, Rayobyte included, run through these checks:
How are residential IPs sourced? Look for an opt-in SDK or app programme with clear user
consent and compensation, and ask which partner apps are involved.
Does the provider publish an ethics or sourcing policy, and has it been audited or certified (for
example AppEsteem or ISO 27001)?
What KYC does the provider apply to customers, and which target categories are restricted?
Strict onboarding is a good sign, not an inconvenience.
How does it handle abuse reports, and is there a named legal entity and jurisdiction behind the
service?
Can you get contractual assurances, such as a data-processing agreement, if your compliance
team needs them?
Bottom line

NetNut is no longer a provider you can plan around, so the real decision is which network replaces it. Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget and teams that also need datacenter or ISP IPs, starts at $3.50/GB (1-49 GB), and offers check current offer. Test it on your own targets for a day, compare cost per successful request with your old NetNut baseline, and move production traffic in stages.
Rayobyte is the better pick for:
Mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget
Teams that also need datacenter or ISP IPs
US buyers who want a US-based vendor
